doc.title: Oliver Nelson Jr. interviewed by Monk Rowe, via Zoom, September 10, 2020

title: What made his father angry: unprepared players and racism
summary: Unprepared musicians on Sound Pieces, segregation in St. Louis, Black, Brown and Beautiful, and Self Help is Needed.

story.theme_name: Race and segregation in the jazz life
story.community_name: Segregation on the road and the bandstand

blocks.x: What kind of things — I’m going to ask this of him and then I’m going to ask it of you so you have a chance to think — what kind of thing would make your father angry?

Probably lack of preparation for musicians that he had to work with. He would get really pretty upset about that. It’s funny you mentioned “Sound Pieces.” Well you know the piece itself was pretty difficult with the bass clar — [scats]. Well they couldn’t play it. When they first were recording they couldn’t play the piece. He sent them home. And they came back and they had to play it the next day. So that stuff, and then the racial situation in the country really got him upset. There’s a place in St. Louis that, you know, you wanted to get a hamburger but black people had to go around the back. And he really couldn’t stand that kind of thing. That’s why the album he did, “Black, Brown and Beautiful” was so significant. Because he’d learned a couple of things. One thing he learned was that was at a time when you know Africa was the motherland for us African- Americans here in the United States. But the Africans didn’t claim us. We were Americans. And he learned that pretty quickly. He said you know we put stock in this country and we have to be proud of the stock that we have put in this country. And then he did a piece called “Self Help is Needed” actually the IU band is going to play that, I just gave some music to the IU guys a couple of days ago. And I wanted them to play it, especially during these racial times. Because we cannot wait, as African-Americans, for the federal government to do anything. We’ve got to do some things yourself.
